Is the clean energy revolution driving the Global South into a debt crisis?

With the 4th International Conference on Financing for Development Forum underway in Seville, we face a defining global challenge: an annual $4 trillion financing gap threatens progress on the SDGs and a just energy transition.

But this is also a turning point. While clean technologies are more affordable than ever (with 81% of new renewable energy additions more cost-competitive than fossil fuels) less than 15% of clean energy investment reached the Global South in 2023. At the same time, public debt is rising rapidly, threatening to derail both climate and development ambitions. This isn’t just a funding gap; it’s a systemic failure. Yet these signs point to a system on the brink of transformation.

The clean energy revolution is no longer optional; it’s essential. To ensure a fair and inclusive transition, we must act on three fronts:

1️⃣ Reform fossil fuel subsidies: Globally, these reached $1.3 trillion in 2023. Redirecting even a portion of this toward clean energy, health and education could unlock massive development gains - especially where subsidies are untargeted and disproportionately benefit the wealthy.

2️⃣ Redesign public finance frameworks: Mobilizing private capital through blended finance, national development banks, and climate bonds can scale up investments while protecting fiscal space. These tools are key to de-risking investments and scaling renewables in places where markets alone won’t go.

3️⃣ Rebuild global cooperation: This goes beyond aid. We need debt-for-climate swaps, donor-backed guarantees and equitable financing frameworks tailored to the needs of the Global South. Efforts like Egypt’s €54M debt swap with Germany already show what’s possible.

At this FfD Forum, we face a choice: continue financing delay, or fund a just, resilient and sustainable future. The energy transition can either deepen inequality or drive inclusive development. The difference lies in how we choose to finance it.
